common_name: Korin Azalea (Classic Purple-Flowered Satsuki Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Korin is an older Japanese Satsuki cultivar that has thrown multiple named sports, including Hakurin and Hikorin, and remains an important link in several Satsuki breeding lines.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to protect the shallow root system from heat and drought. Korin bears small purple flowers on a compact, small-leaved plant typical of the older Satsuki lines grown for bonsai as well as border and container use. It is best known today as the source of several named color sports, among them Hakurin and Hikorin, both of which arose from its purple-flowered line. As with other Satsuki selections, flowering comes later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas, so prune only right after bloom finishes since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.
sources: Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Hikorin is a Japanese-bred sport of the older Satsuki cultivar Korin, sharing that parentage with the related sport Hakurin.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root zone cool and evenly moist. Hikorin arose as a sport of Korin, carrying a related purple flower color, and is grown mainly among Satsuki collectors alongside its sibling sport Hakurin. Its small leaves and compact, slow-growing habit make it well suited to bonsai training as well as container and border planting. Like other Satsuki azaleas, it flowers later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica types and should be pruned only right after bloom, since next year's buds set soon afterward.
sources: Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

common_name: Eiga-no-Homare Azalea (Large Pink-and-Red Satsuki Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Eiga-no-Homare is an older Japanese Satsuki cultivar registered in 1992, best known as the parent of the 1989 sport Mibu-no-Hana.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system evenly moist through summer heat. Eiga-no-Homare carries large flowers with a pink ground overlaid by red secondary markings, a pattern passed down to its sport Mibu-no-Hana. It is grown today mostly by Satsuki collectors who value it as a foundational link in several named breeding lines rather than as a widely sold landscape plant. As with other Satsuki selections, it flowers later than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas, so prune only immediately after bloom since next year's buds form soon afterward.
sources: Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

common_name: Aikoku Azalea (Large White-and-Purple Classic Satsuki Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Aikoku is an older Satsuki cultivar bred from Kaho and Tanima-no-Yuki and is the parent of the 1939 bicolor sport Shugetsu (Autumn Moon).

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to protect the shallow root system from drought and heat. Aikoku bears large white-and-purple flowers and is grown both as a garden plant in its own right and as the parent of the bicolor sport Shugetsu, also known as Autumn Moon. Its vigorous habit and large bloom size make it a long-standing favorite among older Satsuki selections still found in specialist collections. Like other Satsuki azaleas, it flowers later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica types, so prune only right after bloom finishes since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.
sources: Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a sheltered woodland site with dappled shade and protection from wind and late frost; native to high-elevation forests of Yunnan, Tibet, and northern Myanmar.

directions: Rhododendron sinogrande carries the largest simple leaves of any rhododendron, often two feet or more long, glossy dark green above and covered in silvery-white to fawn indumentum beneath. Trusses of pale cream to yellow, sometimes crimson-blotched flowers open in late winter to early spring on a plant that eventually grows into a small tree in favorable climates. It needs a sheltered, humid woodland site out of drying wind, since its enormous leaves tear and brown badly in exposure, and it is only reliably hardy where winters stay mild and summers stay cool and moist. Grow in deep, humus-rich, acidic soil and water generously through dry spells, as the shallow root system cannot reach far for moisture.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Rhododendron species database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a sheltered woodland site with dappled shade and protection from wind and late frost; native to the Naga Hills of Manipur in northeastern India.

directions: Rhododendron macabeanum bears broad, leathery, dark green leaves up to a foot long with gray to fawn felted indumentum on their undersides, among the most striking foliage of any large-leaf rhododendron species. Rounded trusses of bell-shaped, pale to deep yellow flowers, sometimes with a dark purple basal blotch, open in early to mid spring on mature plants grown in cool, humid woodland gardens. It is somewhat hardier than many of its big-leaf relatives but still needs shelter from wind and strong sun, which scorch its large leaves. Plant in deep, acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and dappled shade, and allow ample room since it eventually becomes a substantial small tree.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Rhododendron species database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a sheltered woodland site with dappled shade and protection from wind and late frost; native to the eastern Himalaya from Nepal to Bhutan.

directions: Rhododendron falconeri is grown chiefly for its handsome foliage: thick, deeply veined leaves up to a foot long, glossy dark green above and coated in a thick rust-brown to cinnamon felt of indumentum beneath. Rounded trusses of creamy-yellow to pale pink, purple-blotched flowers open in mid-spring, but the plant takes many years to reach flowering size and is prized in collector gardens as much for its peeling, cinnamon-colored bark and dramatic leaves. It needs a sheltered woodland position out of drying wind and strong midday sun, with cool, humid summers for best performance. Grow in deep, humus-rich, acidic soil kept consistently moist, and allow generous space as it slowly develops into a small tree.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Rhododendron species database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a sheltered woodland site with dappled shade and protection from wind and late frost; native to the eastern Himalaya from Nepal to Sikkim and Bhutan.

directions: Rhododendron grande, one of the classic large-leaved species first introduced from the Himalaya in the nineteenth century, carries long, leathery leaves with a silvery-white sheen of indumentum on their undersides that catches the light in woodland settings. Large, loose trusses of pale cream to blush-pink flowers with a crimson basal blotch open in early-to-mid spring on plants that eventually grow into substantial small trees. It is among the more tender big-leaf species and needs a sheltered, humid site free of hard frost and drying wind to thrive. Grow in deep, acidic, humus-rich soil with consistent moisture and dappled overhead shade, siting it where its dramatic winter leaf-droop and spring flowering can be enjoyed at close range.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Rhododendron species database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a sheltered woodland site with dappled shade and protection from wind and late frost; native to the eastern Himalaya at high elevation from Nepal to Bhutan and southeastern Tibet.

directions: Rhododendron hodgsonii is grown for its thick, stiffly leathery, deeply veined leaves, which curve under at the margins and show a fawn to gray suede-like indumentum beneath, held on handsome gray, peeling-barked stems. Dense, rounded trusses of rose-purple to magenta flowers open in early-to-mid spring, appearing before many companion big-leaf species since it grows at the highest elevations of the group and is somewhat more cold-tolerant as a result. It still needs shelter from drying wind and late frost, which can damage both new foliage and flower buds. Grow in deep, acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture in a cool woodland setting, allowing room for it to form a substantial multi-stemmed large shrub to small tree.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Rhododendron species database
